title: Presentism as an Empirical Hypothesis
kind: primary journal article; author-hosted published-layout copy, directly read
version: Philosophy of Science 80(5) (2013) 1101-1111; eleven-page public copy, not publisher-collated; SHA256 c93ca072e14c4fd0f1c638ff960db17847231479ec9bf168cf0d69f9644bb054
locator: Section 4 'An Alternative Ontological Principle of Unity', printed pp. 1104-1105: laws play a constitutive role in constituting entities as genuine unities; billiard-ball collision example: total quantity of motion conserved and redistributed determinately, making whole and parts genuine unities; persistence through change without essential properties or haecceities. Footnote 3: 'unity' used neutrally for simple things, composite things, and the totality.
assumptions: Law-constitutive approach stated and used, explicitly not argued for in this article
Newton's laws supply the principle of unity instead of spacetime
conclusion: Author claims Newton's physics contains a law-constitutive alternative principle of ontological unity covering simple things, composites, and parts; on its basis a presentism compatible with taking SR seriously remains an open empirical hypothesis.
proof_status: Complete short article read; author's own statement that the law-constitutive view is asserted here, not defended; Newton scholarship not audited.
dependencies: Brading 2011, 2012 (composite systems, law-constitutive approach), referenced not newly read
open_questions: Which independent criterion determines a sustaining extent for a given interacting system
Whether interacting composite unity covers diachronic signal loops, not just instantaneous third-law interactions
relevance: Primary Brading unity doctrine read directly before attribution; controls what her law-constitutive unity does and does not say about interacting parts and diachronic organization.
limits: Selected-authority only for the Newton history; no subsystem criterion supplied by the source; our carrier-loop criterion is not attributed to her.

title: Physically Locating the Present: A Case of Reading Physics as a Contribution to Philosophy
kind: primary journal article; author-hosted published-layout copy, complete short article read directly
version: Studies in History and Philosophy of Science 50 (2015) 13-19; DOI 10.1016/j.shpsa.2014.09.007; nine-page PDF including journal header page (coordinator ledger lists a seven-page copy at the same URL); SHA256 7caceae74aebe28d1775561cd307dce50f912570eb1a7f9a709d70c699b08f6b
locator: Section 4 printed pp. 15-16: first-law conservation constitutes simple bodies; interacting collection forms composite whole in virtue of conserving total quantity and direction of motion; third law gives necessary conditions for part-hood and sufficient conditions for parts' determinacy. Section 5 printed pp. 16-18: proposal 'identify the present of any given unity with the spatiotemporal region that is dynamically necessary to sustain it'; P1** clauses (a) less than entire universe, (b) less than the thing's entire history; presents are local and 'not transitive among systems and their subsystems'; empirical question whether genuine subsystems exist (p. 18).
assumptions: Law-constitutive approach to unity adopted from her earlier work
conclusion: Author proposes a system-relative, dynamically determined, non-transitive present; whether subsystems with sub-universal extents exist is left as an empirical hypothesis requiring dynamics beyond special relativity.
proof_status: Whole article read; proposal is programmatic by her own statement; no sustaining-extent criterion or subsystem theorem given.
dependencies: Brown 2005 chapter connection acknowledged; Brading 2011-2013; Stein 1968; none newly audited
open_questions: Which activity sustains a system and why its extent has existential import
How approximate sustaining regions are to be interpreted
relevance: Strongest primary source proposal for organization-constituted presents; pins exactly what the coordinator apparatus is testing and bars attributing our criterion or contrasts to her.
limits: Her sustaining-region proposal is not accompanied by a criterion; our intervention battery, SCC machinery and negative results are ours.

title: Organisational closure in biological organisms
kind: primary journal article; HAL author-final version read directly
version: History and Philosophy of the Life Sciences 32(2-3) (2010) 269-288; HAL halshs-00792436v1 (submitted 2018-09-19); SHA256 e9122359f75f3756d87c0d8180376d803f7af4c2020763b6d3e62e9f8a955d27; HAL pagination, journal body not collated
locator: Section 2: constraints as material configurations whose dynamics do not determine the configuration (asymmetrical constraint); flame example. Section 3 pp. 6-8: working definition - a system is organisationally closed if constituted by structures C1..Cn acting as constraints such that for each Ci (at least some of) the boundary conditions required for its maintenance are determined by the immediate action of another constraint Cj whose maintenance depends in turn on Ci; three features: (1) partial closure, (2) must involve constraints, not only constrained processes - billiard-ball example is a causal cycle, not closure, (3) direct constraint without intermediate constraints; river/bed and water-cycle counterexamples ruled out; Section 4: closure vs minimal dissipative self-maintenance.
assumptions: Biological scope: organisms in far-from-equilibrium conditions
Constraints as a distinct causal regime on top of physicochemical laws
conclusion: Authors argue organizational closure is a necessary condition for biological organization but underdetermines organismhood; causal cycles of constrained processes with externally given constraints do not realize closure.
proof_status: Complete paper read; conceptual definitions, not formal theorems.
dependencies: Kauffman 2000 work-constraint cycle; Pattee; Mossio et al. 2009; cited not newly read
open_questions: Whether any externally maintained artifact can satisfy closure without carrier regeneration
relevance: Nearest process/organizational-closure primary for the unity criterion; supplies the exact causal-cycle-versus-closure distinction applied to the carrier loop in RESULT.md section 2.
limits: No claim about passive feedback apparatus; our adaptation of their vocabulary to the loop is flagged as a departure, not attributed.

title: Biological organisation as closure of constraints
kind: primary journal article; open-repository version, selected formal sections read directly
version: Journal of Theoretical Biology 372 (2015) 179-191; DOI 10.1016/j.jtbi.2015.02.029; downloaded file cover cites HAL hal-01192916v1 via the hal-01135879 URL; 29-page repository copy, SHA256 088b08923df6e5b19228a0fac78bdaec112beb9cfdf659bf4cac9f66625cac55; repository pagination
locator: Section 3 Definition 1 (Constraint): conditions I (asymmetry of the process outcome with/without C) and II (temporal symmetry of the aspects of C relevant to its causal power) at a specific time scale. Section 4 Definition 2 (Dependence between constraints): two time scales considered jointly; C2 constraint at scale tau2 on a process producing aspects of C1 relevant to its constraint role at tau1; generative/dependent vocabulary. Section 4 Definition 3 (Direct dependence). Section 5 Definition 4 (Closure): each Ci depends directly on at least one other constraint in the set and is generative for at least one other; strict closure adds non-splitability; closure as multiscale network 'cannot be described at a given point in time'; footnote 25 distinguishes closure from a cycle of processes (hydrologic cycle); Section 6: constraints subject to closure define the system boundary; footnote 27: closure does not define organism.
assumptions: Time-scale separation between process scale and constraint production/maintenance scale
Biological motivation; framework claimed general for organized systems
conclusion: Authors supply the formal closure definitions used by the autonomy theory and argue the closed set of constraints defines the system and its boundary.
proof_status: Definitions and surrounding argument read directly; the paper's formal results not independently re-derived.
dependencies: Mossio et al. 2013 constraint definition; Saborido et al. 2011; cited not newly read
open_questions: Whether closure can be ascribed below/above organism level without further specifications (their open section 6 question)
relevance: Canonical formal criterion against which the carrier loop is tested in RESULT.md; source of the exact definitions and of the closure-is-not-at-an-instant point used against reconstruction shortcuts.
limits: HAL copy pagination differs from journal; biological scope; our use redefines 'dependence' for passive carriers and says so.

title: Closure of Constraints and the Individuation of Causal Systems in Biology
kind: primary handbook chapter; CC-BY-NC-ND open-access copy read directly
version: Chapter 15 of The Routledge Handbook of Causality and Causal Methods (Illari and Russo eds.), title page 'First published 2025', ISBN 978-1-032-26019-8 (hbk); chapter DOI 10.4324/9781003528937-24; 16-page OAPEN copy SHA256 267c66b707147a5da6f2972a094fb4cc425fd6a239f01db1e8b0dd66bd3d224e; OpenAlex also lists a 2024 Routledge eBooks record for the same DOI (metadata discrepancy recorded)
locator: Section 15.1: systems individuated on the basis of causal knowledge. Section 15.2: constraint definition quoting Mossio et al. 2013 (conservation and causal power at the relevant time scale, p. 5); dependence between constraints defined as replacement/repair dependence (p. 6); closure = every constraint both dependent and enabling (p. 6, Figure 15.2). Section 15.4 pp. 9-11: functional individuation - an item is internal iff it is both a dependent and an enabling constraint; fire-in-savanna and bacterium examples; Moreno and Mossio 2015 p. 23 quoted: closure is context-dependent with respect to external boundary conditions; degree-of-openness ratio proposal (p. 10); individuality in degrees inverse to openness. Section 15.5: processual view; diachronic reidentification via preserved topology of constraint relations and/or functional roles (pp. 12-13).
assumptions: Theory of biological autonomy (Moreno and Mossio 2015) as background
Functional rather than physical boundary determination
conclusion: Authors apply closure of constraints to individuate living causal systems, determine boundaries functionally, and propose graded individuality via openness.
proof_status: Complete chapter read; conceptual application, no formal theorems reproduced.
dependencies: Montevil and Mossio 2015; Moreno and Mossio 2015; Mossio et al. 2013; Kaiser and Krickel 2023; cited not newly read
open_questions: Diachronic dynamics of individuality and robustness ranking (authors' own open questions)
relevance: Newest nearest work applying closure criteria to individuation and boundary questions; source of the internal-item test (enabling AND dependent) and the graded openness idea adapted in RESULT.md.
limits: Biological scope throughout; no artifact or physics-apparatus case; OAPEN copy not collated with the print book.
